profile.summary: A mid-level Engineering Manager for app build typically leads one or more teams shipping application features and services. They own delivery, team health, hiring input, execution quality, and day-to-day engineering practices. They work closely with product, design, QA, platform, and senior engineering leaders, balancing people management with planning, technical trade-offs, and cross-team coordination.

known_challenges.text: Balancing delivery pressure with coaching, feedback, and team development.
Managing dependencies with product, design, QA, and platform teams that can block app delivery.
Switching from solving problems personally to creating clarity and accountability through others.
Protecting team morale when roadmap churn, incidents, or deadlines disrupt planned work.
Maintaining engineering quality while being pushed for faster feature output.

recommended_question_themes.why: This role is judged heavily on whether teams can ship reliably despite changing priorities and dependencies.

recommended_question_themes.theme: Team health, motivation, and sustainable pace
recommended_question_themes.why: Managers at this level often absorb delivery pressure, and team strain shows up before it becomes attrition or burnout.
Their impact increasingly comes from growing engineers, handling uneven performance, and building stronger day-to-day ownership.
App build work depends on tight coordination with product, design, QA, and adjacent engineering teams.
They need to keep standards high while making pragmatic calls on speed, scope, and technical debt.

terminology.meaning: Choosing work for the next delivery cycle.
Refining upcoming work so it is ready to build.
A regular cadence for shipping changes.
Tracking work blocked by other teams or systems.
Changing what ships to protect time or quality.
Regular manager-report conversations about work and support.
Progress in skills, scope, and level expectations.
Clear input on strengths, gaps, and impact.
Handing off ownership, not just tasks.
The interview process used to assess candidates.
Past shortcuts that slow future development.
Automated build, test, and release pipeline.
Peer checking of changes before merge.
A production problem affecting users or systems.
Logs, metrics, and traces used to understand systems.

listen_for: Whether they talk about outcomes through the team or keep reverting to their own hands-on fixes.
How clearly they name delivery risks, blockers, and dependency patterns.
Whether quality issues are framed as isolated mistakes or system-level process problems.
Shifts in tone around roadmap changes, interrupts, or repeated deadline pressure.
How specifically they talk about developing engineers versus just assigning work.
avoid: Assuming they should still be the main technical problem-solver on the team.
Treating missed dates as purely an execution failure without examining dependency and scope churn.
Pushing people topics aside because delivery feels more urgent.
Using generic leadership advice that ignores the realities of shipping app work across functions.
